theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Decrees of God and Providence
doctrine: The Decrees of God and Providence
summary: God’s eternal plan; his sovereignty over all things; providence as personal and purposeful
readingInstruction: Read Ephesians 1:11, Romans 11:33-36, and Job 42:1-6. Read all three as a single statement about God’s purposes: that he works all things according to his will, that his ways are beyond tracing out, and that Job’s answer to such a God is to say, “I know that you can do all things.”
settingTheScene: You have just finished the book of Job, and now you pause. This is a doctrinal day, a chance to step back from the story and think about what the Bible teaches about God’s rule over the world. Job’s book raises a question that every believer eventually faces: if God is in control, why does he allow evil and suffering? You will not find a full answer here. But the Bible teaches clearly that God is sovereign, that he is good, and that he is not the author of sin. Learning to hold these truths together is part of growing up in the faith.
observation: Ephesians 1:11 says that God “works all things according to the counsel of his will.” The word “all” is the key.
The context is salvation. We “have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things” (Ephesians 1:11).
Romans 11:33 cries out, “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!”
Paul asks, “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Romans 11:34). He is quoting Isaiah 40:13, and the next verse echoes Job 41:11.
“For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen” (Romans 11:36).
In Job 42:2, Job says, “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted.”
In Job 42:3, he admits, “I have uttered what I did not understand, things too wonderful for me, which I did not know.”
Job 42:5-6 describes his new sight and his repentance.
doctrinalFocus:
The Christian church has long taught that God has a plan for the world and carries it out. Theologians call the plan God’s decree and the carrying out of it providence. The Westminster Confession puts it this way: God, “from all eternity, did by the most wise and holy counsel of his own will, freely and unchangeably ordain whatsoever comes to pass.” It then adds three careful clarifications. God is not the author of sin. No violence is done to the will of creatures. And the freedom and responsibility of secondary causes are not removed but established.

Providence has three parts. First, God preserves his creation. “In him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). If God stopped sustaining the world for a moment, it would cease to exist. Second, God concurs with the actions of his creatures. Everything that happens involves real creatures acting, and God’s rule is in and through them. Third, God governs, directing everything toward his purposes.

The book of Job shows all of this at work. Look at chapter 1. The Sabeans raid, fire falls from heaven, the Chaldeans attack, a great wind strikes the house. Each of these is a real event with real agents, and Satan stands behind them, permitted but limited. And yet Job says, “The LORD has taken away.” That is not because Job is confused. It is because he sees that God is above the causes. He is the first cause, and the others are secondary. The same event can be the sin of the Sabeans and the permission of God. Genesis 50:20 says it clearly in Joseph’s words: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” The cross is the supreme example: “This Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). God’s plan and human guilt are both real.

How should we hold these together? We should not claim to understand more than the Bible says. Paul does not try to resolve it. He says, “Oh, the depth!” The right response to this doctrine is worship. And it is a comfort. If God rules everything, then nothing in your life is outside his hand, and nothing is wasted. The Heidelberg Catechism says that all things come to us “not by chance but from his fatherly hand.”

There is a caution, too. This doctrine is meant to comfort sufferers, not to be used on them. The friends of Job tried to explain suffering with theology, and God rebuked them. Speak about providence to yourself in your own pain, and to others only with great gentleness.
interpretation:
Job’s final answer in 42:2 is a confession of the doctrine we have been discussing. “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted.” It is not the cry of someone who has found a satisfying argument. It is the settled conviction of someone who has been brought low and has seen God.

What makes it remarkable is when Job says it. He says it without having received an explanation. He still does not know about the courtroom scene in heaven. He still does not know why his children died. But he has seen enough of God to know that God’s plan will stand. And that is enough.

This is also how Paul speaks in Romans 11. He has just spent three chapters wrestling with how God will bring about the salvation of Israel and the nations. When he reaches the end, he does not offer a final theory. He breaks into praise. The plan is too deep. “To him be glory forever.” The doctrine of providence is not meant to end in a diagram. It is meant to end in a doxology.

The lines in Ephesians 1:11 should be read in context. Paul says that God works all things according to the counsel of his will in order to say something about the security of believers. We have an inheritance. We were chosen. God is working, and he will finish what he started. Providence, in the Bible, is mostly a message of hope for the people of God.
connection: Proverbs 16:9 says, “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps.” Psalm 115:3 says, “Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases.” Jesus said that not even a sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father (Matthew 10:29). Isaiah 46:9-10 declares, “My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose.”
application:
First, take a hard thing in your life and ask, “What does it mean that God is sovereign over this?” Write one sentence and one prayer.

Second, notice the difference between the doctrine as a comfort and the doctrine as a weapon. Resolve to use it only for the first.

Third, spend time in worship. Read Romans 11:33-36 aloud as a prayer, and let it end in praise.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that nothing in your life is outside his hand.
Tell him about a part of his ways you do not understand, and ask him for trust.
Give him the glory he is owed.
